**Bulle** (French:[[byl]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ef/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Aemines2-bulle.wav/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Aemines2-bulle.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q150_(fra)-Aemines2-bulle.wav "File:LL-Q150 (fra)-Aemines2-bulle.wav"); [Arpitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpitan_language "Arpitan language"): _Bulo_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-3)[[ˈbylo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Franco-Proven%C3%A7al "Help:IPA/Franco-Provençal")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/c/c1/Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg/Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg "File:Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg")) is a [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Switzerland "Municipalities of Switzerland") in the district of [Gruyère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruy%C3%A8re_(district) "Gruyère (district)") in the [canton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantons_of_Switzerland "Cantons of Switzerland") of [Fribourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fribourg_(canton) "Fribourg (canton)") in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"). In January 2006 Bulle incorporated the formerly independent municipality of [La Tour-de-Trême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Tour-de-Tr%C3%AAme "La Tour-de-Trême").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Ancient times

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Ancient times")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Bulle_Stadt.jpg/250px-Bulle_Stadt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulle_Stadt.jpg)

Houses and the castle in Bulle

Bulle is first mentioned in the 9th century as _Butulum_. In 1200 it was mentioned as _Bollo_. The municipality was formerly known by its German name _Boll_; however, that name is no longer used.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

Very little is known about the early history of the Bulle area. In 1995, a large [grave mound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus") from the early [Hallstatt period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallstatt_culture "Hallstatt culture") was partially excavated. The grave mound lies about 300 m (980 ft) from the hill on which the church was later built.

### Middle ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Middle ages")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Bulle_15.JPG/250px-Bulle_15.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulle_15.JPG)

The old town of Bulle

During the [Early Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Middle_Ages "Early Middle Ages") it was the home of a [parish church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish_church "Parish church") that covered a large [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish"). This Church of St. Eusebius was probably built in the 6th or 7th century by the [Bishop of Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Lausanne "Bishop of Lausanne"). The church is mentioned several times between 852 and 875. In the 9th century, the parish was split into several independent parishes. As the parish shrunk in size, the church gradually lost its former importance, but it remained the center of the [Decanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deanery "Deanery") of Ogo until the 16th century. The deanery covered the whole Saanen valley to Treyvaux, the [Jaun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaun_Pass "Jaun Pass") and Sionge valleys and extended west to Glâne. Bulle probably came under the secular power of the Bishop of Lausanne as early as the 6th century, and together with [Avenches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenches "Avenches") and [Curtilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtilles "Curtilles") formed the territory originally owned by the bishop.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

Since the counts of Gruyères also possessed sovereign rights in Bulle, there were numerous conflicts between the counts and the bishop in the 12th, 13th and 14th centuries. Since these conflicts were always decided in favor of the bishop, the counts eventually lost all rights in Bulle. Even by the 12th century, Bulle was an important regional economic center. In 1195/96, Count Rudolph closed the [market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_town "Market town") in Gruyère and extended his support to the older market in Bulle. At that time, the town was a collection of homesteads, which surrounded a church and maybe had a castle near them. In the 13th century the bishops recognized that the town was crucial to their income and to administer and defend the surrounding region. Bishop Boniface erected a city wall surrounding a rectangular town with two lanes and four rows of houses in 1231–39. A little later, possibly under the episcopate of William de Champvent (1273–1301), the castle was built was in the southeast of the city. The main building of the castle was a 33-metre-high (108 ft) tower that dominated the south gate and the surrounding plain. Throughout the Middle Ages, the bishops appointed two officers, the [castellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castellan "Castellan") and the mayor to rule the town. Throughout the 13th to 15th centuries, the noble de Bulle family held the office of mayor. Although citizens of Bulle are mentioned in 1195/96, they first had an organization in the 14th century testifies. Starting at end of the 12th century, individual freedoms, rights and privileges were often conferred on the citizens of the town and in general the citizens of Bulle had the same privileges as citizens in Lausanne. Starting around 1350, many of the towns in the Saanen valley between Gruyere and Arconciel lost most of their historic importance and population. However, due to Bulle's favorable location, its infrastructure and the support of the bishops, it remained an important regional center. It was also able to recover quickly from a devastating fire in 1447.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

#### Early modern era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early modern era")]

A turning point in the Bulle's history was during the [Burgundian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundian_Wars "Burgundian Wars"). On 16 January 1476 it entered into an alliance with the city of [Fribourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fribourg "Fribourg"). Due to the treaty, it was not plundered by the victorious Swiss after the [Battle of Morat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morat "Battle of Morat") (22 June 1476). In 1536, as the [Bernese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern "Bern") conquered the Vaud, Bishop Sébastien de Montfalcon fled from Lausanne to Fribourg and placed himself and Bulle under the protection of that city. With Fribourg's protection, Bulle was able to remain [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church "Roman Catholic Church"). However, the protection of Fribourg was transformed into domination in 1537. The citizens were placed under a Fribourg appointed [bailiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailiff "Bailiff") who ruled over the former episcopal lands from the castle in Bulle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

The period from 1536 to 1798 was reasonably quiet. The town expanded slightly beyond the city walls near the upper gate. While it was politically powerless, it became an economic center for cheese production and trade. It was the hub for most cheeses that were exported to France. In the 17th century the chapel and the statue erected in her (Notre-Dame-de-Pitié or de Compassion) became a [pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") destination. In 1665 the [Capuchins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Friars_Minor_Capuchin "Order of Friars Minor Capuchin") took over the property, enlarged and embellished the chapel and built convent buildings on the site of the hospital. The hospital moved to the vicinity of the upper gate. The shrine attracted many pilgrims from the Counties of Burgundy and Savoy. In the 18th century, its popularity began to slowly wane. In 1750-51 a new building replaced the parish church of Saint-Pierre-aux-Liens, which had become too small. In 1763–1768, the bailiff's quarters and the audience hall in the castle were expanded and renovated.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

#### 18th century to present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 18th century to present")]

Starting at the end of the 18th century, Bulle became important in the cantonal government. Pierre-Nicolas Chenaux, who led a popular uprising against the [Ancien Régime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Modern_Switzerland "Early Modern Switzerland") government in Fribourg in 1781, held meetings before the uprising in Bulle. After the failure of the uprising, several members of the movement went into exile in Paris and founded the Helvétique Club. During the [1798 French invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Switzerland#Collapse "French invasion of Switzerland") many of the residents of Bulle joined the revolutionary cause. By 26 January, a [liberty tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_pole "Liberty pole") was raised in front of the castle and the citizens had selected an oversight committee and drove the governor out of the city. Bulle would have gladly joined the French-supported [Lemanic Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemanic_Republic "Lemanic Republic"), but after the march elections it became part of the [Helvetic Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetic_Republic "Helvetic Republic")'s Canton of Fribourg. Under Fribourg, the town of [Gruyères](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruy%C3%A8res "Gruyères") was chosen as the seat of the district, instead of Bulle. Bulle also became deeply indebted during the French occupation of 1798–1802. It became a staging post for troops marching from the north into Italy and had to pay for both troops stationed in Bulle as well as troops marching through its lands.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

On 2 April 1805 an enormous fire destroyed almost the entire city. It was quickly rebuilt, and most of the medieval streets were retained. However, one of the four rows of houses was not rebuilt to make room for a large marketplace. The town [granary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granary "Granary") was quickly rebuilt, followed by the town hall in 1808, and the rebuilt church in 1816.

During the entire 19th century Bulle was often in sharp opposition to the conservative cantonal government during the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_and_Regeneration_(Switzerland) "Restoration and Regeneration (Switzerland)") (1814–1830). They supported a liberal cantonal constitution during the Regeneration movement that prevailed in 1831. After 1840 the Conservatives gained back power in the cantonal government, which gave new impetus to the radical opposition, and Bulle was one of its most important centers. In January 1847 there was an open rebellion in Bulle. On 6 January 1847 the mayor was imprisoned in the castle. Three days later, on 9 January, an armed group marched from Bulle toward Fribourg, but returned to the town when they were only half way there. Following the [Sonderbund War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonderbund_War "Sonderbund War"), (brief civil war where a group of cantons unhappy with domination by Bern attempted to leave the Swiss Confederation and were stopped by a Federal army) the new Cantonal Constitution of 1848 made Bulle the capital of the Gruyère district. During the 1853 elections, which punished the radicals for their political excesses, the city was the scene of violence. Violent clashes in Bulle between radicals and conservatives lasted the entire 19th century. At the same time both parties were trying to distinguish themselves with ambitious projects. The radicals built a rail line between Bulle and Romont, established the Banque Populaire de la Gruyère in 1853, opened the radical _[La Gruyère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Gruy%C3%A8re\_(newspaper) "La Gruyère (newspaper)")_ newspaper in 1882, and in 1893 constructed their own electric company. The Conservatives opened the "Le Fribourgeois" paper in 1867, established the Crédit Gruyérien bank in 1867, and built the Chemins de fer de la Gruyère électriques in 1903–1912.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

Aerial view (1954)

From the mid-19th century to 1970, the Radical party possessed a majority in the town council, while the Conservatives were always in the minority. In 1948, the Socialists gained two seats, which they lost in 1950, but won again in 1958 and 1966. Between 1970 and 1996 the council consisted of four Radicals, three Socialists and Social Democrats, and two Christian Democrats. During the Second World War, Bulle was the site of a major riot, the Bulle Riot. On 23 November 1944, five federal inspectors, who were investigating the illicit trade in meat, were attacked by a mob and forced to flee to the castle (which was the district administration building) for safety. In October 1945 the Federal Court met in Fribourg, and in the presence of the entire Swiss press handed down fourteen convictions for the rioters.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Le_p%C3%A2quier_-_montbarry_-_bulle_-_gruyere_-_switzerland_-_immobilier_-_prestige_-_villa_-_construction.jpg/250px-Le_p%C3%A2quier_-_montbarry_-_bulle_-_gruyere_-_switzerland_-_immobilier_-_prestige_-_villa_-_construction.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_p%C3%A2quier_-_montbarry_-_bulle_-_gruyere_-_switzerland_-_immobilier_-_prestige_-_villa_-_construction.jpg)

View from Le Pâquier-Montbarry, near Bulle

Bulle has an area, as of 2013[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), of 23.86 square kilometers (9.21 mi 2). Of this area, 10.03 km 2 (3.87 mi 2) or 42.0% is used for agricultural purposes, while 7.55 km 2 (2.92 mi 2) or 31.6% is forested. Of the rest of the land, 6.04 km 2 (2.33 mi 2) or 25.3% is settled (buildings or roads), 0.14 km 2 (0.054 mi 2) or 0.6% is either rivers or lakes and 0.08 km 2 (20 acres) or 0.3% is unproductive land.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-BFS_land-5)

Of the built up area, industrial buildings made up 4.0% of the total area while housing and buildings made up 12.5% and transportation infrastructure made up 6.5%. Power and water infrastructure as well as other special developed areas made up 1.3% of the area. Out of the forested land, 30.2% of the total land area is heavily forested and 1.5% is covered with orchards or small clusters of trees. Of the agricultural land, 10.1% is used for growing crops and 20.6% is pastures and 11.3% is used for alpine pastures. All the water in the municipality is flowing water.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-BFS_land-5)

The municipality is the capital of the Gruyère district. It is located on a hill at an elevation of 770 meters (2,530 ft) above the left side of the Trême river.

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Bulle_19.JPG/250px-Bulle_19.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulle_19.JPG)

Fountain and green space in the old town of Bulle

Bulle has a population (as of December 2020[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit)) of 24,412.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-Stat2020_FR-7)As of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), 29.8% of the population are resident foreign nationals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS_superweb-8) Over the last 10 years (2000–2010) the population has changed at a rate of 27.2%. Migration accounted for 24.2%, while births and deaths accounted for 3.8%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

Most of the population (as of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit)) speaks [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") (9,492 or 85.1%) as their first language, [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language") is the second most common (488 or 4.4%) and [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") is the third (345 or 3.1%). There are 125 people who speak [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and 2 people who speak [Romansh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romansh_language "Romansh language").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

As of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), the population was 48.6% male and 51.4% female. The population was made up of 5,693 Swiss men (31.2% of the population) and 3,185 (17.4%) non-Swiss men. There were 6,605 Swiss women (36.1%) and 2,790 (15.3%) non-Swiss women.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-FR_STAT-11) Of the population in the municipality, 2,917 or about 26.2% were born in Bulle and lived there in 2000. There were 3,896 or 34.9% who were born in the same canton, while 1,227 or 11.0% were born somewhere else in Switzerland, and 2,642 or 23.7% were born outside of Switzerland.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), children and teenagers (0–19 years old) make up 25.3% of the population, while adults (20–64 years old) make up 60.5% and seniors (over 64 years old) make up 14.2%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 4,730 people who were single and never married in the municipality. There were 5,034 married individuals, 798 widows or widowers and 587 individuals who are divorced.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 6,000 private households in the municipality, and an average of 2.3 persons per household.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9) There were 1,575 households that consist of only one person and 311 households with five or more people. In 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), a total of 4,502 apartments (89.5% of the total) were permanently occupied, while 373 apartments (7.4%) were seasonally occupied and 155 apartments (3.1%) were empty.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-Housing-12)As of 2009[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), the construction rate of new housing units was 13.1 new units per 1000 residents.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

As of 2003[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit) the average price to rent an average apartment in Bulle was 1026.06 [Swiss francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_franc "Swiss franc") (CHF) per month (US$820, £460, €660 approx. exchange rate from 2003). The average rate for a one-room apartment was 514.78 CHF (US$410, £230, €330), a two-room apartment was about 731.83 CHF (US$590, £330, €470), a three-room apartment was about 940.67 CHF (US$750, £420, €600) and a six or more room apartment cost an average of 1525.37 CHF (US$1220, £690, €980). The average apartment price in Bulle was 91.9% of the national average of 1116 CHF.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-BFS_rent-13) The vacancy rate for the municipality, in 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), was 1.18%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

### Sights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sights")]

Downtown Bulle is made up of many shops and offices, a train/bus station (TPF) (with regular service to nearby Fribourg), and an old château that was converted into a prison. A sculpture of a bull sits in a traffic circle by the bus station, showing the emblematic animal for which Bulle is named.

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Politics")]

In the [2011 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Swiss_federal_election "2011 Swiss federal election") the most popular party was the [SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_of_Switzerland "Social Democratic Party of Switzerland") which received 32.8% of the vote. The next three most popular parties were the [SVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_People's_Party "Swiss People's Party") (18.6%), the [CVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Democratic_People's_Party_of_Switzerland "Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland") (16.9%) and the [FDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FDP.The_Liberals "FDP.The Liberals") (16.2%).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-2011_Election-16)

The SPS gained an additional 5.1% of the vote from the [2007 Federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Swiss_federal_election "2007 Swiss federal election") (27.6% in 2007 vs 32.8% in 2011). The SVP moved from third in 2007 (with 21.6%) to second in 2011, the CVP moved from second in 2007 (with 22.0%) to third and the FDP retained about the same popularity (18.2% in 2007). A total of 4,617 votes were cast in this election, of which 128 or 2.8% were invalid.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-17)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

As of 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), Bulle had an unemployment rate of 4.9%. As of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 74 people employed in the [primary economic sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_sector_of_the_economy "Primary sector of the economy") and about 22 businesses involved in this sector. 3,932 people were employed in the [secondary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_sector_of_the_economy "Secondary sector of the economy") and there were 167 businesses in this sector. 6,381 people were employed in the [tertiary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy "Tertiary sector of the economy"), with 737 businesses in this sector.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9) There were 5,480 residents of the municipality who were employed in some capacity, of which females made up 45.1% of the workforce.

In 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit) the total number of [full-time equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-time_equivalent "Full-time equivalent") jobs was 8,850. The number of jobs in the primary sector was 56, of which 49 were in agriculture and 6 were in forestry or lumber production. The number of jobs in the secondary sector was 3,784 of which 2,411 or (63.7%) were in manufacturing, 5 or (0.1%) were in mining and 1,250 (33.0%) were in construction. The number of jobs in the tertiary sector was 5,010. In the tertiary sector; 1,631 or 32.6% were in wholesale or retail sales or the repair of motor vehicles, 319 or 6.4% were in the movement and storage of goods, 452 or 9.0% were in a hotel or restaurant, 70 or 1.4% were in the information industry, 472 or 9.4% were the insurance or financial industry, 517 or 10.3% were technical professionals or scientists, 471 or 9.4% were in education and 492 or 9.8% were in health care.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-18)

In 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 4,927 workers who commuted into the municipality and 2,232 workers who commuted away. The municipality is a net importer of workers, with about 2.2 workers entering the municipality for every one leaving.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-commuter-19) Of the working population, 8% used public transportation to get to work, and 66.1% used a private car.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Transportation")]

Main article: [Bulle railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle_railway_station "Bulle railway station")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/20061126S41_537176.jpg/250px-20061126S41_537176.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20061126S41_537176.jpg)

Bulle train station

Bulle is the centre of operations of the former [Chemins de fer fribourgeois Gruyère–Fribourg–Morat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemins_de_fer_fribourgeois_Gruy%C3%A8re%E2%80%93Fribourg%E2%80%93Morat "Chemins de fer fribourgeois Gruyère–Fribourg–Morat") network, now managed by [Transports publics Fribourgeois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transports_publics_Fribourgeois "Transports publics Fribourgeois"). At Bulle are the administrative headquarters, workshops, and, within its modern transportation hub and station, connections between meter and standard gauge lines as well as to many bus lines. Transfer to the wide-ranging trains of the Montreux-Oberland Bernois (Panorama Express) takes place at nearby Montbovon, which provides a convenient connection for travelers from Montreux to the Gruyère line's popular Chocolate Express.

Of the rest of the population, there were 54 [members of an Orthodox church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodoxy#Christianity "Orthodoxy") (or about 0.48% of the population), there were 8 individuals (or about 0.07% of the population) who belonged to the [Christian Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Catholic_Church_of_Switzerland "Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland"), and there were 246 individuals (or about 2.21% of the population) who belonged to another Christian church. ## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Education")]

In Bulle about 3,207 or (28.8%) of the population have completed non-mandatory [upper secondary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Switzerland#Secondary "Education in Switzerland"), and 1,134 or (10.2%) have completed additional higher education (either [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Switzerland "List of universities in Switzerland") or a _[Fachhochschule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fachhochschule "Fachhochschule")_). Of the 1,134 who completed tertiary schooling, 57.4% were Swiss men, 25.7% were Swiss women, 10.1% were non-Swiss men and 6.9% were non-Swiss women.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

The Canton of Fribourg school system provides one year of non-obligatory [Kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindergarten "Kindergarten"), followed by six years of Primary school. This is followed by three years of obligatory lower Secondary school where the students are separated according to ability and aptitude. Following the lower Secondary students may attend a three or four year optional upper Secondary school. The upper Secondary school is divided into [gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnasium_(school) "Gymnasium (school)") (university preparatory) and vocational programs. After they finish the upper Secondary program, students may choose to attend a Tertiary school or continue their [apprenticeship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apprenticeship "Apprenticeship").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-20)

During the 2010–11 school year, there were a total of 6,205 students attending 325 classes in Bulle. A total of 3,029 students from the municipality attended any school, either in the municipality or outside of it. There were 11 kindergarten classes with a total of 193 students in the municipality. The municipality had 58 primary classes and 1,243 students. During the same year, there were 84 lower secondary classes with a total of 1,682 students. There were 79 vocational upper Secondary classes and were 47 upper Secondary classes, with 938 upper Secondary students and 1,166 vocational upper Secondary students The municipality had 18 specialized Tertiary classes and were 28 non-university Tertiary classes, with 838 non-university Tertiary students and 145 specialized Tertiary students.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-FR_STAT-11)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 1,680 students in Bulle who came from another municipality, while 200 residents attended schools outside the municipality.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-commuter-19)

Bulle is home to the _Bibliothèque de Bulle_ library. The library has (as of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit)) 78,000 books or other media, and loaned out 131,270 items in the same year. It was open a total of 260 days with average of 31 hours per week during that year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-21)

**Bulle** (French:[[byl]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ef/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Aemines2-bulle.wav/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Aemines2-bulle.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q150_(fra)-Aemines2-bulle.wav "File:LL-Q150 (fra)-Aemines2-bulle.wav"); [Arpitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpitan_language "Arpitan language"): _Bulo_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-3)[[ˈbylo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Franco-Proven%C3%A7al "Help:IPA/Franco-Provençal")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/c/c1/Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg/Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg "File:Frp-greverin-Bulo.ogg")) is a [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Switzerland "Municipalities of Switzerland") in the district of [Gruyère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruy%C3%A8re_(district) "Gruyère (district)") in the [canton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantons_of_Switzerland "Cantons of Switzerland") of [Fribourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fribourg_(canton) "Fribourg (canton)") in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"). In January 2006 Bulle incorporated the formerly independent municipality of [La Tour-de-Trême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Tour-de-Tr%C3%AAme "La Tour-de-Trême").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Ancient times

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Ancient times")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Bulle_Stadt.jpg/250px-Bulle_Stadt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulle_Stadt.jpg)

Houses and the castle in Bulle

Bulle is first mentioned in the 9th century as _Butulum_. In 1200 it was mentioned as _Bollo_. The municipality was formerly known by its German name _Boll_; however, that name is no longer used.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

Very little is known about the early history of the Bulle area. In 1995, a large [grave mound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus") from the early [Hallstatt period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallstatt_culture "Hallstatt culture") was partially excavated. The grave mound lies about 300 m (980 ft) from the hill on which the church was later built.

### Middle ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Middle ages")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Bulle_15.JPG/250px-Bulle_15.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulle_15.JPG)

The old town of Bulle

During the [Early Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Middle_Ages "Early Middle Ages") it was the home of a [parish church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish_church "Parish church") that covered a large [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish"). This Church of St. Eusebius was probably built in the 6th or 7th century by the [Bishop of Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Lausanne "Bishop of Lausanne"). The church is mentioned several times between 852 and 875. In the 9th century, the parish was split into several independent parishes. As the parish shrunk in size, the church gradually lost its former importance, but it remained the center of the [Decanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deanery "Deanery") of Ogo until the 16th century. The deanery covered the whole Saanen valley to Treyvaux, the [Jaun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaun_Pass "Jaun Pass") and Sionge valleys and extended west to Glâne. Bulle probably came under the secular power of the Bishop of Lausanne as early as the 6th century, and together with [Avenches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenches "Avenches") and [Curtilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtilles "Curtilles") formed the territory originally owned by the bishop.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

Since the counts of Gruyères also possessed sovereign rights in Bulle, there were numerous conflicts between the counts and the bishop in the 12th, 13th and 14th centuries. Since these conflicts were always decided in favor of the bishop, the counts eventually lost all rights in Bulle. Even by the 12th century, Bulle was an important regional economic center. In 1195/96, Count Rudolph closed the [market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_town "Market town") in Gruyère and extended his support to the older market in Bulle. At that time, the town was a collection of homesteads, which surrounded a church and maybe had a castle near them. In the 13th century the bishops recognized that the town was crucial to their income and to administer and defend the surrounding region. Bishop Boniface erected a city wall surrounding a rectangular town with two lanes and four rows of houses in 1231–39. A little later, possibly under the episcopate of William de Champvent (1273–1301), the castle was built was in the southeast of the city. The main building of the castle was a 33-metre-high (108 ft) tower that dominated the south gate and the surrounding plain. Throughout the Middle Ages, the bishops appointed two officers, the [castellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castellan "Castellan") and the mayor to rule the town. Throughout the 13th to 15th centuries, the noble de Bulle family held the office of mayor. Although citizens of Bulle are mentioned in 1195/96, they first had an organization in the 14th century testifies. Starting at end of the 12th century, individual freedoms, rights and privileges were often conferred on the citizens of the town and in general the citizens of Bulle had the same privileges as citizens in Lausanne. Starting around 1350, many of the towns in the Saanen valley between Gruyere and Arconciel lost most of their historic importance and population. However, due to Bulle's favorable location, its infrastructure and the support of the bishops, it remained an important regional center. It was also able to recover quickly from a devastating fire in 1447.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

#### Early modern era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early modern era")]

A turning point in the Bulle's history was during the [Burgundian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundian_Wars "Burgundian Wars"). On 16 January 1476 it entered into an alliance with the city of [Fribourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fribourg "Fribourg"). Due to the treaty, it was not plundered by the victorious Swiss after the [Battle of Morat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morat "Battle of Morat") (22 June 1476). In 1536, as the [Bernese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern "Bern") conquered the Vaud, Bishop Sébastien de Montfalcon fled from Lausanne to Fribourg and placed himself and Bulle under the protection of that city. With Fribourg's protection, Bulle was able to remain [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church "Roman Catholic Church"). However, the protection of Fribourg was transformed into domination in 1537. The citizens were placed under a Fribourg appointed [bailiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailiff "Bailiff") who ruled over the former episcopal lands from the castle in Bulle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

The period from 1536 to 1798 was reasonably quiet. The town expanded slightly beyond the city walls near the upper gate. While it was politically powerless, it became an economic center for cheese production and trade. It was the hub for most cheeses that were exported to France. In the 17th century the chapel and the statue erected in her (Notre-Dame-de-Pitié or de Compassion) became a [pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") destination. In 1665 the [Capuchins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Friars_Minor_Capuchin "Order of Friars Minor Capuchin") took over the property, enlarged and embellished the chapel and built convent buildings on the site of the hospital. The hospital moved to the vicinity of the upper gate. The shrine attracted many pilgrims from the Counties of Burgundy and Savoy. In the 18th century, its popularity began to slowly wane. In 1750-51 a new building replaced the parish church of Saint-Pierre-aux-Liens, which had become too small. In 1763–1768, the bailiff's quarters and the audience hall in the castle were expanded and renovated.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

#### 18th century to present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 18th century to present")]

Starting at the end of the 18th century, Bulle became important in the cantonal government. Pierre-Nicolas Chenaux, who led a popular uprising against the [Ancien Régime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Modern_Switzerland "Early Modern Switzerland") government in Fribourg in 1781, held meetings before the uprising in Bulle. After the failure of the uprising, several members of the movement went into exile in Paris and founded the Helvétique Club. During the [1798 French invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Switzerland#Collapse "French invasion of Switzerland") many of the residents of Bulle joined the revolutionary cause. By 26 January, a [liberty tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_pole "Liberty pole") was raised in front of the castle and the citizens had selected an oversight committee and drove the governor out of the city. Bulle would have gladly joined the French-supported [Lemanic Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemanic_Republic "Lemanic Republic"), but after the march elections it became part of the [Helvetic Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetic_Republic "Helvetic Republic")'s Canton of Fribourg. Under Fribourg, the town of [Gruyères](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruy%C3%A8res "Gruyères") was chosen as the seat of the district, instead of Bulle. Bulle also became deeply indebted during the French occupation of 1798–1802. It became a staging post for troops marching from the north into Italy and had to pay for both troops stationed in Bulle as well as troops marching through its lands.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

On 2 April 1805 an enormous fire destroyed almost the entire city. It was quickly rebuilt, and most of the medieval streets were retained. However, one of the four rows of houses was not rebuilt to make room for a large marketplace. The town [granary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granary "Granary") was quickly rebuilt, followed by the town hall in 1808, and the rebuilt church in 1816.

During the entire 19th century Bulle was often in sharp opposition to the conservative cantonal government during the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_and_Regeneration_(Switzerland) "Restoration and Regeneration (Switzerland)") (1814–1830). They supported a liberal cantonal constitution during the Regeneration movement that prevailed in 1831. After 1840 the Conservatives gained back power in the cantonal government, which gave new impetus to the radical opposition, and Bulle was one of its most important centers. In January 1847 there was an open rebellion in Bulle. On 6 January 1847 the mayor was imprisoned in the castle. Three days later, on 9 January, an armed group marched from Bulle toward Fribourg, but returned to the town when they were only half way there. Following the [Sonderbund War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonderbund_War "Sonderbund War"), (brief civil war where a group of cantons unhappy with domination by Bern attempted to leave the Swiss Confederation and were stopped by a Federal army) the new Cantonal Constitution of 1848 made Bulle the capital of the Gruyère district. During the 1853 elections, which punished the radicals for their political excesses, the city was the scene of violence. Violent clashes in Bulle between radicals and conservatives lasted the entire 19th century. At the same time both parties were trying to distinguish themselves with ambitious projects. The radicals built a rail line between Bulle and Romont, established the Banque Populaire de la Gruyère in 1853, opened the radical _[La Gruyère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Gruy%C3%A8re\_(newspaper) "La Gruyère (newspaper)")_ newspaper in 1882, and in 1893 constructed their own electric company. The Conservatives opened the "Le Fribourgeois" paper in 1867, established the Crédit Gruyérien bank in 1867, and built the Chemins de fer de la Gruyère électriques in 1903–1912.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

From the mid-19th century to 1970, the Radical party possessed a majority in the town council, while the Conservatives were always in the minority. In 1948, the Socialists gained two seats, which they lost in 1950, but won again in 1958 and 1966. Between 1970 and 1996 the council consisted of four Radicals, three Socialists and Social Democrats, and two Christian Democrats. During the Second World War, Bulle was the site of a major riot, the Bulle Riot. On 23 November 1944, five federal inspectors, who were investigating the illicit trade in meat, were attacked by a mob and forced to flee to the castle (which was the district administration building) for safety. In October 1945 the Federal Court met in Fribourg, and in the presence of the entire Swiss press handed down fourteen convictions for the rioters.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS-4)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Le_p%C3%A2quier_-_montbarry_-_bulle_-_gruyere_-_switzerland_-_immobilier_-_prestige_-_villa_-_construction.jpg/250px-Le_p%C3%A2quier_-_montbarry_-_bulle_-_gruyere_-_switzerland_-_immobilier_-_prestige_-_villa_-_construction.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_p%C3%A2quier_-_montbarry_-_bulle_-_gruyere_-_switzerland_-_immobilier_-_prestige_-_villa_-_construction.jpg)

View from Le Pâquier-Montbarry, near Bulle

Bulle has an area, as of 2013[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), of 23.86 square kilometers (9.21 mi 2). Of this area, 10.03 km 2 (3.87 mi 2) or 42.0% is used for agricultural purposes, while 7.55 km 2 (2.92 mi 2) or 31.6% is forested. Of the rest of the land, 6.04 km 2 (2.33 mi 2) or 25.3% is settled (buildings or roads), 0.14 km 2 (0.054 mi 2) or 0.6% is either rivers or lakes and 0.08 km 2 (20 acres) or 0.3% is unproductive land.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-BFS_land-5)

Of the built up area, industrial buildings made up 4.0% of the total area while housing and buildings made up 12.5% and transportation infrastructure made up 6.5%. Power and water infrastructure as well as other special developed areas made up 1.3% of the area. Out of the forested land, 30.2% of the total land area is heavily forested and 1.5% is covered with orchards or small clusters of trees. Of the agricultural land, 10.1% is used for growing crops and 20.6% is pastures and 11.3% is used for alpine pastures. All the water in the municipality is flowing water.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-BFS_land-5)

The municipality is the capital of the Gruyère district. It is located on a hill at an elevation of 770 meters (2,530 ft) above the left side of the Trême river.

Bulle has a population (as of December 2020[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit)) of 24,412.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-Stat2020_FR-7)As of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), 29.8% of the population are resident foreign nationals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-HDS_superweb-8) Over the last 10 years (2000–2010) the population has changed at a rate of 27.2%. Migration accounted for 24.2%, while births and deaths accounted for 3.8%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

Most of the population (as of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit)) speaks [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") (9,492 or 85.1%) as their first language, [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language") is the second most common (488 or 4.4%) and [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") is the third (345 or 3.1%). There are 125 people who speak [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and 2 people who speak [Romansh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romansh_language "Romansh language").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

As of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), the population was 48.6% male and 51.4% female. The population was made up of 5,693 Swiss men (31.2% of the population) and 3,185 (17.4%) non-Swiss men. There were 6,605 Swiss women (36.1%) and 2,790 (15.3%) non-Swiss women.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-FR_STAT-11) Of the population in the municipality, 2,917 or about 26.2% were born in Bulle and lived there in 2000. There were 3,896 or 34.9% who were born in the same canton, while 1,227 or 11.0% were born somewhere else in Switzerland, and 2,642 or 23.7% were born outside of Switzerland.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), children and teenagers (0–19 years old) make up 25.3% of the population, while adults (20–64 years old) make up 60.5% and seniors (over 64 years old) make up 14.2%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 4,730 people who were single and never married in the municipality. There were 5,034 married individuals, 798 widows or widowers and 587 individuals who are divorced.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 6,000 private households in the municipality, and an average of 2.3 persons per household.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9) There were 1,575 households that consist of only one person and 311 households with five or more people. In 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), a total of 4,502 apartments (89.5% of the total) were permanently occupied, while 373 apartments (7.4%) were seasonally occupied and 155 apartments (3.1%) were empty.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-Housing-12)As of 2009[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), the construction rate of new housing units was 13.1 new units per 1000 residents.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

As of 2003[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit) the average price to rent an average apartment in Bulle was 1026.06 [Swiss francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_franc "Swiss franc") (CHF) per month (US$820, £460, €660 approx. exchange rate from 2003). The average rate for a one-room apartment was 514.78 CHF (US$410, £230, €330), a two-room apartment was about 731.83 CHF (US$590, £330, €470), a three-room apartment was about 940.67 CHF (US$750, £420, €600) and a six or more room apartment cost an average of 1525.37 CHF (US$1220, £690, €980). The average apartment price in Bulle was 91.9% of the national average of 1116 CHF.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-BFS_rent-13) The vacancy rate for the municipality, in 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), was 1.18%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

### Sights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sights")]

Downtown Bulle is made up of many shops and offices, a train/bus station (TPF) (with regular service to nearby Fribourg), and an old château that was converted into a prison. A sculpture of a bull sits in a traffic circle by the bus station, showing the emblematic animal for which Bulle is named.

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Politics")]

In the [2011 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Swiss_federal_election "2011 Swiss federal election") the most popular party was the [SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_of_Switzerland "Social Democratic Party of Switzerland") which received 32.8% of the vote. The next three most popular parties were the [SVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_People's_Party "Swiss People's Party") (18.6%), the [CVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Democratic_People's_Party_of_Switzerland "Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland") (16.9%) and the [FDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FDP.The_Liberals "FDP.The Liberals") (16.2%).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-2011_Election-16)

The SPS gained an additional 5.1% of the vote from the [2007 Federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Swiss_federal_election "2007 Swiss federal election") (27.6% in 2007 vs 32.8% in 2011). The SVP moved from third in 2007 (with 21.6%) to second in 2011, the CVP moved from second in 2007 (with 22.0%) to third and the FDP retained about the same popularity (18.2% in 2007). A total of 4,617 votes were cast in this election, of which 128 or 2.8% were invalid.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-17)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Economy")]

As of 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), Bulle had an unemployment rate of 4.9%. As of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 74 people employed in the [primary economic sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_sector_of_the_economy "Primary sector of the economy") and about 22 businesses involved in this sector. 3,932 people were employed in the [secondary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_sector_of_the_economy "Secondary sector of the economy") and there were 167 businesses in this sector. 6,381 people were employed in the [tertiary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy "Tertiary sector of the economy"), with 737 businesses in this sector.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9) There were 5,480 residents of the municipality who were employed in some capacity, of which females made up 45.1% of the workforce.

In 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit) the total number of [full-time equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-time_equivalent "Full-time equivalent") jobs was 8,850. The number of jobs in the primary sector was 56, of which 49 were in agriculture and 6 were in forestry or lumber production. The number of jobs in the secondary sector was 3,784 of which 2,411 or (63.7%) were in manufacturing, 5 or (0.1%) were in mining and 1,250 (33.0%) were in construction. The number of jobs in the tertiary sector was 5,010. In the tertiary sector; 1,631 or 32.6% were in wholesale or retail sales or the repair of motor vehicles, 319 or 6.4% were in the movement and storage of goods, 452 or 9.0% were in a hotel or restaurant, 70 or 1.4% were in the information industry, 472 or 9.4% were the insurance or financial industry, 517 or 10.3% were technical professionals or scientists, 471 or 9.4% were in education and 492 or 9.8% were in health care.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-18)

In 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 4,927 workers who commuted into the municipality and 2,232 workers who commuted away. The municipality is a net importer of workers, with about 2.2 workers entering the municipality for every one leaving.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-commuter-19) Of the working population, 8% used public transportation to get to work, and 66.1% used a private car.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-SFSO-9)

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Transportation")]

Main article: [Bulle railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle_railway_station "Bulle railway station")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/20061126S41_537176.jpg/250px-20061126S41_537176.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20061126S41_537176.jpg)

Bulle train station

Bulle is the centre of operations of the former [Chemins de fer fribourgeois Gruyère–Fribourg–Morat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemins_de_fer_fribourgeois_Gruy%C3%A8re%E2%80%93Fribourg%E2%80%93Morat "Chemins de fer fribourgeois Gruyère–Fribourg–Morat") network, now managed by [Transports publics Fribourgeois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transports_publics_Fribourgeois "Transports publics Fribourgeois"). At Bulle are the administrative headquarters, workshops, and, within its modern transportation hub and station, connections between meter and standard gauge lines as well as to many bus lines. Transfer to the wide-ranging trains of the Montreux-Oberland Bernois (Panorama Express) takes place at nearby Montbovon, which provides a convenient connection for travelers from Montreux to the Gruyère line's popular Chocolate Express.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Education")]

In Bulle about 3,207 or (28.8%) of the population have completed non-mandatory [upper secondary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Switzerland#Secondary "Education in Switzerland"), and 1,134 or (10.2%) have completed additional higher education (either [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Switzerland "List of universities in Switzerland") or a _[Fachhochschule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fachhochschule "Fachhochschule")_). Of the 1,134 who completed tertiary schooling, 57.4% were Swiss men, 25.7% were Swiss women, 10.1% were non-Swiss men and 6.9% were non-Swiss women.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-STAT2000-10)

The Canton of Fribourg school system provides one year of non-obligatory [Kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindergarten "Kindergarten"), followed by six years of Primary school. This is followed by three years of obligatory lower Secondary school where the students are separated according to ability and aptitude. Following the lower Secondary students may attend a three or four year optional upper Secondary school. The upper Secondary school is divided into [gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnasium_(school) "Gymnasium (school)") (university preparatory) and vocational programs. After they finish the upper Secondary program, students may choose to attend a Tertiary school or continue their [apprenticeship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apprenticeship "Apprenticeship").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-20)

During the 2010–11 school year, there were a total of 6,205 students attending 325 classes in Bulle. A total of 3,029 students from the municipality attended any school, either in the municipality or outside of it. There were 11 kindergarten classes with a total of 193 students in the municipality. The municipality had 58 primary classes and 1,243 students. During the same year, there were 84 lower secondary classes with a total of 1,682 students. There were 79 vocational upper Secondary classes and were 47 upper Secondary classes, with 938 upper Secondary students and 1,166 vocational upper Secondary students The municipality had 18 specialized Tertiary classes and were 28 non-university Tertiary classes, with 838 non-university Tertiary students and 145 specialized Tertiary students.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-FR_STAT-11)

As of 2000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit), there were 1,680 students in Bulle who came from another municipality, while 200 residents attended schools outside the municipality.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-commuter-19)

Bulle is home to the _Bibliothèque de Bulle_ library. The library has (as of 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bulle&action=edit)) 78,000 books or other media, and loaned out 131,270 items in the same year. It was open a total of 260 days with average of 31 hours per week during that year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulle#cite_note-21)
