## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Governance")]

### Civic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Civic")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/The_Buttercross%2C_Ludlow.jpg/250px-The_Buttercross%2C_Ludlow.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Buttercross,_Ludlow.jpg)

The Buttercross, built in 1743–1746, at the top of Broad Street and the highest point of the medieval town (the site of the High Cross); historically this spot was used as a benchmark for road distances to Ludlow.

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/The_Guildhall_building%2C_Mill_Street%2C_Ludlow._-_geograph.org.uk_-_1337410.jpg/250px-The_Guildhall_building%2C_Mill_Street%2C_Ludlow._-_geograph.org.uk_-_1337410.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Guildhall_building,_Mill_Street,_Ludlow._-_geograph.org.uk_-_1337410.jpg)

[Ludlow Guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Guildhall "Ludlow Guildhall")

Ludlow is a [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_England "Civil parishes in England") with a [town council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_councils_in_England "Town councils in England") and a mayor. Ludlow was a [borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_borough "Ancient borough") from 1461 to 1974 (becoming a [municipal borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_borough "Municipal borough") in 1835 and a [rural borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_borough "Rural borough") in 1967); the borough encompassed the same area as Ludlow's [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish") until the mid-late 19th century. Its borough status meant Ludlow was largely autonomous from the hundred of [Munslow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munslow_(hundred) "Munslow (hundred)") which it lay in.

Wider local government was provided by [Ludlow Rural District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Rural_District "Ludlow Rural District") from 1894 (this rural district absorbed the borough of Ludlow in 1967, causing the change in status to a rural borough) until 1974 when [South Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shropshire "South Shropshire") District Council (with Ludlow as its seat) took over along with [Shropshire County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_County_Council "Shropshire County Council") in a two-tier arrangement. Rural boroughs were abolished in 1974 and Ludlow's [borough status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "Borough status in the United Kingdom") at that point ended. The district councils of Shropshire were abolished in 2009 and the county now has a [unitary authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_authority "Unitary authority") called [Shropshire Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Council "Shropshire Council"), based in Shrewsbury. The South Shropshire District Council's offices at Stone House on Corve Street were gradually emptied of local government staff until their sale in 2014.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-101)

The town council is based at [Ludlow Guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Guildhall "Ludlow Guildhall") on Mill Street, a grade I listed building,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-102) which was the home of the town's [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_court "County court") and magistrates' courts until their closure in 2011.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-103) There was a Town Hall, situated in the Square, which was built in 1887–1888 and demolished in March 1986;[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-104) it featured prominently just prior to its demolition in the 1985 television drama _[Blott on the Landscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blott\_on\_the\_Landscape "Blott on the Landscape")_. The other notable civic building in the centre of town is the [Buttercross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Buttercross "Ludlow Buttercross") (named as it was the butter market at the site of the medieval High Cross); it was the home of the town council after the demolition of the Town Hall and prior to the closure of the courts. It is now an 'interpretation centre' for the town's architectural heritage.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-105)

### Electoral arrangements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Electoral arrangements")]

The boundaries of Ludlow's wards and electoral divisions were most recently reviewed in 2008.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-106)

Fifteen councillors sit on the town council, representing seven [wards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wards_in_the_United_Kingdom "Wards in the United Kingdom"), and elections (when contested) are held every four years (at the same time as elections to Shropshire Council). The seven wards changed slightly in 2008, retaining their previous names and number of councillors they each return – they are (with the number of town councillors returned given): Rockspring (2), Hayton (2), Bringewood (2), Corve (2), Whitcliffe (2), Gallows Bank (3), and Clee View (2).

Ludlow together with nearby parishes comprise three electoral divisions, each returning one councillor to Shropshire Council in elections held every four years, the [most recent being in 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Shropshire_Council_election#Ludlow_East "2021 Shropshire Council election"). The electoral divisions comprise:

*   Ludlow North (the wards of Corve, Whitcliffe and Bringewood together with the parish of [Bromfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromfield,_Shropshire "Bromfield, Shropshire"))
*   Ludlow East (the wards of Hayton, Clee View and Rockspring)
*   Ludlow South (Gallows Bank and the parishes of [Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire"), [Richard's Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard's_Castle "Richard's Castle"), [Ashford Bowdler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashford_Bowdler "Ashford Bowdler") and [Ashford Carbonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashford_Carbonell "Ashford Carbonell")).

### Civil parishes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Civil parishes")]

Ludford is a separate [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_England "Civil parishes in England"), with its own parish council, and covers the adjoining places of [Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire"), Foldgate, Steventon, [the Sheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sheet "The Sheet") and Rocks Green. Until 1901 an area of land at the foot of Old Street, called [Holdgate Fee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holdgate_Fee "Holdgate Fee"), was a detached part of Ludford parish in the town itself. Ludlow Castle was a parish of its own, contained within the castle's walls and the immediate hillside; it was abolished in 1901 and ceded to Ludlow's civil parish.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-107) Other than Ludford, the only other civil parish in the present-day that neighbours Ludlow is [Bromfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromfield,_Shropshire "Bromfield, Shropshire").

The civil parish of [East Hamlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Hamlet "East Hamlet"), created in 1884 covered a limited area to the east of the town; this parish was largely absorbed by Ludlow's parish as the town expanded into it (in 1901, 1934 and finally in 1987 when it was abolished). Ludlow's parish in 1901 expanded into Ludford to the east (taking in Holdgate Fee and the Steventon New Road area); another two expansions into Ludford in 1934 involved taking in the Whitcliffe (which had been acquired by the burgesses of Ludlow already in the 13th century)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-108) and a further part to the east (the Gallows Bank area). 1934 also saw a significant expansion of the Ludlow parish west into Bromfield's parish, on both sides of the Teme; this coupled with the inclusion of Whitcliffe constitutes the western, essentially rural part to Ludlow's civil parish in the present day.

### Parliament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Parliament")]

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Coat_of_arms_of_Ludlow.png/250px-Coat_of_arms_of_Ludlow.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coat_of_arms_of_Ludlow.png)

The coat of arms of Ludlow date to the creation of the parliamentary borough and pay homage to [Richard, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_of_York,_3rd_Duke_of_York "Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York"). It displays the white lion of the [Earl of March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_March "Earl of March") surrounded by three [white roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Rose_of_York "White Rose of York") of the [House of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_York "House of York")

For representation to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom"), Ludlow falls within the [South Shropshire constituency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shropshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "South Shropshire (UK Parliament constituency)"), which has its origins in the [Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Ludlow (UK Parliament constituency)")[parliamentary borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_borough "Parliamentary borough") constituency created in 1473, and which until 1868 returned two [burgesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_(title) "Burgess (title)") to Parliament.

In modern times, the Ludlow constituency came to cover a large area of southern Shropshire including [Bridgnorth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgnorth "Bridgnorth") and after constituency boundary changes was redesignated [South Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shropshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "South Shropshire (UK Parliament constituency)") ahead of the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election") when the current member, [Stuart Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Anderson_(politician) "Stuart Anderson (politician)") of the [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(United_Kingdom) "Conservative Party (United Kingdom)"), was elected.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-109)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Economy")]

McConnel Limited, a manufacturer of hedge cutting and verge mowing machinery, is based in Ludlow, occupying a seven-acre industrial site in the Temeside/Weeping Cross area of the town known as the Temeside Works.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-110) The company claims to be the innovator of the first tractor-mounted hedge cutting machine (produced in 1945) and a leading producer of reach flail mower hedge and verge mowing power-arm technology.

### Market

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Market")]

The town has regular outdoor markets held on Castle Square, an area that was enlarged in 1986 with the demolition of the Town Hall (which was also known as Market Hall). General markets are held on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays. Specialist markets (examples being crafts, antiques, local produce) are held on occasional Thursdays and Sundays. They are run by the town council.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-111)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Education")]

Ludlow has two primary schools for children aged 5–11 and a secondary school – the [Ludlow Church of England School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Church_of_England_School "Ludlow Church of England School") — for pupils aged 11–16.

[Ludlow College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_College "Ludlow College") is a sixth form college in the town centre, formed by the merger of the town's boys grammar school and girls high school. Prior to its merger with [Herefordshire College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herefordshire_and_Ludlow_College "Herefordshire and Ludlow College") in 2012 it was one of the oldest educational institutions in the country, dating back some 800 years.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-112)

## Health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Health")]

[Ludlow Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Hospital "Ludlow Hospital") is an NHS community hospital at the junction of Gravel Hill and New Road. It had until recently several inpatient and outpatient departments and wards, as well as a minor injuries unit.

There are two doctors' surgeries in the town, both just off Upper Galdeford.

## Emergency services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Emergency services")]

The [Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Fire_and_Rescue_Service "Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service") have a fire station on Weeping Cross Lane, staffed by [retained firefighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retained_firefighter "Retained firefighter").

[West Mercia Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Mercia_Police "West Mercia Police") have a police station on Lower Galdeford. Its front counter closed in 2015.

Voluntary aid society, the [British Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Red_Cross "British Red Cross"), has a hall in the Smithfield car park, just off Lower Galdeford, and adjacent to the fire station.

## Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Religion")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/St._Peter%27s_Catholic_Church%2C_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_628950.jpg/250px-St._Peter%27s_Catholic_Church%2C_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_628950.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St._Peter's_Catholic_Church,_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_628950.jpg)

St Peter's church, built in the late 1930s in the neo-Byzantine and plain Romanesque styles, is the town's Roman Catholic church

There are two [Church of England parishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish_(Church_of_England) "Parish (Church of England)") in Ludlow and two Church of England churches – the large and historic [St Laurence's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Laurence's_Church,_Ludlow "St Laurence's Church, Ludlow") in the centre of the town – and the 19th century St John's Church on Gravel Hill. Within St Laurence's Church are the St John's, Lady and St Catherine's chapels.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-113) Ludford has its own Church of England [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_parish "Ecclesiastical parish") and church, dedicated to St Giles.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-114)

Ludlow falls within the Church of England's [Diocese of Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Hereford "Diocese of Hereford") and between 1981 and 2020 was a suffragan [see](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_see "Episcopal see") with its own [suffragan bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragan_bishop "Suffragan bishop"), the [Bishop of Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Ludlow "Bishop of Ludlow"), the only such bishop in the diocese.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-115) There has long been an [Archdeacon of Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdeacon_of_Ludlow "Archdeacon of Ludlow"), historically known as the Archdeacon of Shropshire, overseeing the other parishes in the southern part of the county (the part of the Hereford diocese that is within Shropshire).

The [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") church of St Peter is on Henley Road.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-116) Construction to a design by the Welsh-based Italian architect [Giuseppe Rinvolucri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Rinvolucri "Giuseppe Rinvolucri") began in 1935, using stone from nearby [Farlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farlow,_Shropshire "Farlow, Shropshire") and building in a neo-Byzantine and plain Romanesque style. The construction also involved novel reinforced concrete technology. The Byzantine design continues inside, with a blue dome with twelve gold-leaf stars representing St Peter and the other Apostles.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-117)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-118) An [Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco "Art Deco")[presbytery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy_house "Clergy house") was built next to the church. [St Mary Magdalene's chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St_Mary_Magdalene_(Ludlow) "Chapel of St Mary Magdalene (Ludlow)"), within the castle, is now a ruin[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-119) although it was restored and roofed in 2018 and is open as a wedding venue.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-120)

Ludlow has a [Methodist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_Church_of_Great_Britain "Methodist Church of Great Britain") church on Broad Street,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-121) a [Quaker Meeting House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker_Meeting_House "Quaker Meeting House") on St Mary's Lane,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-122) a [Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptists_Together "Baptists Together") church at the Rockspring Community Centre,[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-123) and an [Elim Pentecostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elim_Pentecostal_Church "Elim Pentecostal Church") church off the Smithfield car park.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-124)

Two [monastic institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery "Monastery") once existed in Ludlow – one Augustinian ("Austin") Friars on the corner of Lower Galdeford and Weeping Cross Lane, and the other Carmelite ("White") Friars between Linney and Corve Street. Both were [dissolved in 1538](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Monasteries "Dissolution of the Monasteries"). The White Friars site became the town's cemetery in 1824, with a new church constructed, dedicated to St Leonard (a St Leonard's chapel existed on the corner of Corve Street and Linney in medieval times). The St Leonard's graveyard and church still exist but are no longer used for burials or worship (instead the church building is now a commercial premises). The Austin Friars site became the town's livestock market (the Smithfield) and is now a public car park.

**Ludlow** ([/ˈ l ʌ d l oʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/0/00/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Tesco250-Ludlow.wav/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Tesco250-Ludlow.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Tesco250-Ludlow.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Tesco250-Ludlow.wav")[_LUD-loh_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is a [market town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_town "Market town") and [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parish "Civil parish") in south [Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_(district) "Shropshire (district)"), England. It is located 28 miles (45 km) south of [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury "Shrewsbury") and 23 miles (37 km) north of [Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereford "Hereford"), on the [A49 road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A49_road_(Great_Britain) "A49 road (Great Britain)") which bypasses the town. The town is near the confluence of the rivers [Corve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Corve "River Corve") and [Teme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Teme "River Teme").

The oldest part is the [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval")[walled town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall"), founded in the late 11th century after the [Norman conquest of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest"). It is centred on a small hill which lies on the eastern bank of a bend of the River Teme. Situated on this hill are [Ludlow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Castle "Ludlow Castle") and the parish church, [St Laurence's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Laurence's_Church,_Ludlow "St Laurence's Church, Ludlow"), the largest in the county.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-2) From there the streets slope downward to the rivers [Corve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Corve "River Corve") and [Teme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Teme "River Teme"), to the north and south respectively. The town is in a sheltered spot beneath [Mortimer Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortimer_Forest "Mortimer Forest") and the [Clee Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clee_Hills "Clee Hills"), which are clearly visible from the town.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-3)

Ludlow has nearly 500 [listed buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-4) including examples of medieval and [Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_architecture "Tudor architecture")-style [half-timbered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-timbered "Half-timbered") buildings. The town was described by [Sir John Betjeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Betjeman "John Betjeman") as "probably the loveliest town in England".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-5)

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

The 13th century romance [_Fouke le Fitz Waryn_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fouke_le_Fitz_Waryn#Romance_of_Fouke_le_Fitz_Waryn "Fouke le Fitz Waryn") records that Ludlow had been called **Dinam** "for a very long time". It is also known that [Ludlow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Castle "Ludlow Castle") was originally named Dinham Castle when it was constructed in the 11th century, even today the area immediately south of the castle retains the original name.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-7)[Samuel Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Lewis_(publisher) "Samuel Lewis (publisher)") states that while _Leadlowe_ and _Ludlowe_ were the Saxon names for the town, the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Britons "Celtic Britons") name was _Dinam_, which he translates as 'the palace of princes'.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-9) Even in the 18th century, [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") recorded that "the Welch call this town _Llys Tywysog_, which is in English, the Prince's Court."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-10)

_Lodelowe_ was in use for this site before 1138 and comes from the [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English")_hlud-hlǣ_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-Room_2003-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-toponymy75-12) At the time this section of the [River Teme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Teme "River Teme") contained rapids, and so the _hlud_ of _Ludlow_ came from 'the loud waters', while _hlǣw_ meant 'hill'[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-Room_2003-11) or [tumulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-13) Thus the name _Ludlow_ describes a 'place on a hill by the loud waters'. Some time around the 12th century, [weirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weir "Weir") were added along the river, taming these rapid flows.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-14) The hill is that which the town stands on, and a pre-historic burial mound (or barrow) which existed at the eastern summit of the hill (dug up during the expansion of St Laurence's church in 1199) could explain the tumulus variation of the _hlǣw_ element.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-toponymy75-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-poulton-15)[Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire"), a neighbouring and older settlement, situated on the southern bank of the Teme, shares the _hlud_ ('loud waters') element.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-poulton-15)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

See also: [History of Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Shropshire "History of Shropshire") and [Ludlow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Castle "Ludlow Castle")

The town is situated close to [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"), and lies near the midpoint of the 257-kilometre-long (160 mi)[England–Wales border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England%E2%80%93Wales_border "England–Wales border"); it is also very close to the county border between Shropshire and [Herefordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herefordshire "Herefordshire") (neighbouring [Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire") remained part of Herefordshire until 1895). This strategic location invested it with national importance in [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") times, and thereafter with the town being the seat of the [Council of Wales and the Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Wales_and_the_Marches "Council of Wales and the Marches") during its existence (1472 to 1689).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-16)

### Medieval history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Medieval history")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Ludlow_Castle_from_Whitcliffe%2C_2011.jpg/250px-Ludlow_Castle_from_Whitcliffe%2C_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ludlow_Castle_from_Whitcliffe,_2011.jpg)

[Ludlow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Castle "Ludlow Castle"), built in the late 11th century.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Magnificent_stained_glass_window_within_St_Laurence%2C_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1444523.jpg/250px-Magnificent_stained_glass_window_within_St_Laurence%2C_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1444523.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Magnificent_stained_glass_window_within_St_Laurence,_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1444523.jpg)

The [stained glass window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass_window "Stained glass window") above the west door of St Laurence's displays the Lords of Ludlow Castle and most notably four key royals associated with Ludlow during/after the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses"). The praying figures at the foot are (from left to right) [Richard, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_of_York,_3rd_Duke_of_York "Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York"), his son [Edward IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_IV "Edward IV") and his son [Edward V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_V "Edward V") and grandson [Arthur, Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur,_Prince_of_Wales "Arthur, Prince of Wales").

At the time of the [Domesday Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book") survey, the area was part of the large [Stanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanton_Lacy "Stanton Lacy") parish and [manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manorialism "Manorialism"), a possession of [Walter de Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_de_Lacy_(died_1085) "Walter de Lacy (died 1085)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-17) Neither Ludlow nor Dinham are mentioned in the Book, compiled in 1086, although the Book recorded manors and not settlements _per se_. The Book does record a great number of households and taxable value for Stanton, perhaps suggesting that any early settlement by the nascent castle was being counted. Neighbouring places Ludford, the Sheet and Steventon do feature in the Book, as they were manors, proving that they were well-established places by the Norman conquest.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-18) The manor of Stanton came within the [hundred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_(county_division) "Hundred (county division)") of [Culvestan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culvestan "Culvestan"), but during the reign of [Henry I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_I_of_England "Henry I of England") this Saxon hundred was merged into the new [Munslow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munslow_(hundred) "Munslow (hundred)") hundred.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-19)

Walter's son [Roger de Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_de_Lacy "Roger de Lacy") began the construction of [Ludlow Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Castle "Ludlow Castle") on the western [promontory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promontory "Promontory") of the hill about 1075, forming what is now the inner [bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailey_(castle) "Bailey (castle)"). Between about 1090 and 1120, the Chapel of [St. Mary Magdalene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary_Magdalene "St. Mary Magdalene") was built inside the walls, and by 1130 the Great Tower was added to form the [gatehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatehouse "Gatehouse"). About 1170 the larger outer bailey was added to the castle. (The town walls however were not built until the mid-13th century.) The settlement of Dinham grew up alongside the development of the early castle in the late 11th century, with the northern part of this early settlement disturbed by the building of the outer bailey.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-origins-20) Dinham had its own place of worship, the Chapel of St Thomas the Martyr, dedicated to [Thomas Becket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Becket "Thomas Becket") sometime in 1177–1189 when the present chapel replaced an older (late 11th-century) church building.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-21)

During the 12th century, the planned town of Ludlow was formed, in stages, the town providing a useful source of income for successive [Marcher Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcher_Lords "Marcher Lords"), based on rents, fines, and tolls. They developed the town on a regular grid pattern, although this was adapted somewhat to match the local [topography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topography "Topography"), from the late 11th century through the 12th century. The first laid street was along the ridge of the hilltop, what is now Castle Square, High Street and King Street. This formed a wide marketplace (later in-filled by buildings in places) running from the castle gates east across to St Laurence's and the Bull Ring, itself located on the ancient north–south road, now called Corve Street to the north and Old Street to the south. The wide Mill and Broad Streets were added later, as part of a southern grid plan of streets and [burgage plots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgage_plot "Burgage plot") filling the area bounded by Dinham, the new High Street market, Old Street and the Teme to the south.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-origins-20) Originally, Old Street ran down to a [ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_(crossing) "Ford (crossing)") which took the ancient route south across to [Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire"). A bridge was constructed (possibly by [Josce de Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josce_de_Dinan "Josce de Dinan")) at the foot of Broad Street, upstream of the ford, which then replaced the ford; its 15th-century replacement is the present-day [Ludford Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford_Bridge "Ludford Bridge").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-22)

[St Laurence's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Laurence's_Church,_Ludlow "St Laurence's Church, Ludlow"), whose origins are late 11th century, was rebuilt and enlarged (with a bell tower) in 1199-1200[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-origins-20) and became a parish church, with the separation of Ludlow from the [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish") of Stanton Lacy by 1200. The town notably had two schools (a choir and a grammar) in existence c.1200;[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-23)[Ludlow Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Grammar_School "Ludlow Grammar School") remained in existence until 1977, when it became Ludlow College.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-24)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Castle_square_ludlow.jpg/250px-Castle_square_ludlow.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Castle_square_ludlow.jpg)

The town's outdoor market, in Castle Square, photographed from St Laurence's Church

Ludlow Castle was an important border fortification along the [Welsh Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Marches "Welsh Marches"), and one of the largest in the Norman/English ring of castles surrounding Wales. It played a significant role in local, regional and national conflicts such as the [Owain Glyndŵr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owain_Glynd%C5%B5r "Owain Glyndŵr") rebellion, the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses") and the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"). The castle and its adjoining town grew in political importance and in the 15th century the castle became the seat of the [Council of Wales and the Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Wales_and_the_Marches "Council of Wales and the Marches"). It was a temporary home to several holders of the title [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales"), including King [Edward V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_V "Edward V") and [Arthur Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Tudor "Arthur Tudor"), who died there in 1502.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-25)

The site features heavily in the folk-story of [Fulk FitzWarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulk_FitzWarin "Fulk FitzWarin"), outlawed Lord of [Whittington, Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whittington,_Shropshire "Whittington, Shropshire") and a possible inspiration for the _[Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin\_Hood "Robin Hood")_ legend. Fulk is brought up in the castle of [Josce de Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josce_de_Dinan "Josce de Dinan"), and fights for his master against Sir [Gilbert de Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_de_Lacy "Gilbert de Lacy") – these battles are the source of the story of Marion de la Bruyere, the betrayed lover whose ghost is still said to be heard screaming as she plummets from the castle's turrets.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-26)

The first recorded royal permission to maintain defensive town walls was given to the "men of Ludlow" in the [Patent Rolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_Rolls "Patent Rolls") of 1233. The entry is however incomplete and atypical and was not renewed in the usual way. A [murage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murage "Murage") grant was next made in 1260 and renewed regularly over the next two centuries. This time the grant was made by name to [Geoffrey de Genevile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_de_Genevile?action=edit&redlink=1 "Geoffrey de Genevile (page does not exist)"), Lord of Ludlow. From this and other surviving documents it seems that the town walls and gates were in place by 1270.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-train-27) They were constructed about the central part of the community with four main gates and three [postern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postern "Postern") gates. Because the walls were constructed after the development of the town's streets, the positions and names of the four main gates are based on the streets they crossed; the postern gates on the other hand are located by and named after old outlying districts. The 7 gates are (clockwise from the castle; postern gates in _italics_) _Linney_, Corve, _Galdeford_, Old, Broad, Mill and _Dinham_. An eighth unnamed 'portal' gate (smaller than a postern gate) existed in the wall just to the northwest of the castle, now in the gardens of Castle Walk House.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-28) The town walls are largely still in existence, although a section alongside the churchyard of St Lawrence's is, as of 2015, in need of repairs.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-29)

The castle complex continued to expand (a Great Hall, kitchen and living quarters were added) and it gained a reputation as a fortified [palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace "Palace"). In 1306 it passed through marriage to the ambitious [Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Mortimer,_1st_Earl_of_March "Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March"). [Queen Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France") and her son, the young [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III"), were entertained at the castle in 1329.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-30)

### Marcher town

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Marcher town")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Feathers_hotel.jpg/250px-Feathers_hotel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Feathers_hotel.jpg)

The [Feathers Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feathers_Hotel,_Ludlow "Feathers Hotel, Ludlow"), one of Ludlow's more famous timber-framed buildings.

The town prospered, with a population of about 1,725 by 1377,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-medievalpop-31) and sustained a population of about 2,000 for several centuries thereafter. It was a market town; market day was held on every Thursday throughout the 15th century. In particular, it served as a centre for the sale of [wool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool "Wool") and cloth.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-medievalpop-31) It was home to various trades, and in 1372 boasted 12 [trade guilds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilds "Guilds") including [metalworkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalworker "Metalworker"), [shoemakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoemaker "Shoemaker"), butchers, [drapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draper "Draper"), [mercers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercery "Mercery"), tailors, [cooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_(profession) "Cook (profession)"), bakers and probably the most notable in the town, the [religious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_guild "Religious guild")[Palmer's Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmer's_Guild "Palmer's Guild").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-32)

In the mid sixteenth century the London merchant [Sir Rowland Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowland_Hill_(MP) "Rowland Hill (MP)") gave the money for a new bridge over the Teme, and the annual St. Catherine's fair.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-33)

There were [merchants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant "Merchant") of moderate wealth in the town and especially wool merchants, such as [Laurence of Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_of_Ludlow "Laurence of Ludlow"), who lived at nearby [Stokesay Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokesay_Castle "Stokesay Castle"). The collection and sale of wool and the manufacture of cloth continued to be the primary source of wealth until the 17th century.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-34)

This prosperity is expressed in stone masonry, wood carvings and [stained-glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained-glass "Stained-glass") at [St. Laurence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Laurence_Church,_Ludlow "St Laurence Church, Ludlow")'s [parish church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish_church "Parish church"); effectively a [wool church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool_church "Wool church"), it is the largest in [Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire "Shropshire") and a member of the [Greater Churches Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Churches_Group "Greater Churches Group"). Despite the presence of some [Decorated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decorated_Period "Decorated Period") work it is largely [Perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular_Period "Perpendicular Period") in style.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-35) Its size and grandeur has given it the nickname "the [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral "Cathedral") of the Marches", and from 1981 to 2020 there was a [suffragan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragan_bishop "Suffragan bishop")[Bishop of Ludlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Ludlow "Bishop of Ludlow").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-36)

During the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses"), the castle—which he held through his Mortimer inheritance—was one of [Richard, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_of_York,_3rd_Duke_of_York "Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York")'s main strongholds.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-37) The [Lancastrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lancaster "House of Lancaster") forces captured Ludlow in 1459, at the [Rout of Ludford Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rout_of_Ludford_Bridge "Rout of Ludford Bridge"), but the [Yorkists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_York "House of York") won control of England in 1461. The castle became property of the Crown, passing to Richard's son, [Edward IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_IV "Edward IV"). The town rose in prominence under Edward's reign and was incorporated as a [borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_borough "Ancient borough"), and began sending [representatives to Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Ludlow (UK Parliament constituency)"). Edward set up the [Council of Wales and the Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Wales_and_the_Marches "Council of Wales and the Marches") in 1472, headquartering it at Ludlow, and sent his son [Edward, Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_V "Edward V"), to live there, as nominal (being only a young boy) head of the council. It was at Ludlow that the young prince heard the news of his father's death in 1483 and was himself proclaimed King Edward V of England.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-38) It was from Ludlow that Edward V was brought back to London with his young brother, both to be confined in the Tower of London when, after a short period of time, they were never seen again.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/St._Laurence%2C_Ludlow%2C_from_west.jpg/250px-St._Laurence%2C_Ludlow%2C_from_west.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St._Laurence,_Ludlow,_from_west.jpg)

The [Church of St Laurence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Laurence_Church,_Ludlow "St Laurence Church, Ludlow") has Norman origins and expanded throughout the Middle Ages, being a [wool church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wool_church "Wool church"), becoming the largest parish church in Shropshire.

Under [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") the castle continued as the headquarters of the Council of Wales and served as the administration centre for [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales") and the counties along the border, known as the [Welsh Marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Marches "Welsh Marches"). During this period, when the town served as the effective capital of Wales, it was home to many messengers of the king, various clerks and lawyers for settling legal disputes. The town also provided a winter home for local [gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentry "Gentry"), during which time they attended the council court sessions. Henry VII sent his heir [Prince Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur,_Prince_of_Wales "Arthur, Prince of Wales") to Ludlow, where he was joined briefly by his wife [Catherine of Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Aragon "Catherine of Aragon") later to become wife to [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII"). Ludlow Castle was therefore the site of perhaps the most controversial honeymoon in English history, when Catherine's claim that the marriage was never consummated became central to the dispute concerning Henry VIII and Catherine's annulment in 1531.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-39)

Eventually, the council resumed and except for brief interludes, Ludlow continued to host the council until 1689, when it was abolished by [William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England") and [Mary II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_II "Mary II") as part of the [Glorious Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution"). The castle then fell into decay. The structure was poorly maintained and the stone was [pillaged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillage "Pillage"). In 1772 demolition was mooted, but it was instead decided to lease the buildings. Later still it was purchased by the [Earl of Powis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Powis "Earl of Powis"), and together, he and his wife directed the transformation of the castle grounds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-40)

The [Royal Welch Fusiliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Welch_Fusiliers "Royal Welch Fusiliers") were formed by [Henry Herbert, 4th Baron Herbert of Chirbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Herbert,_4th_Baron_Herbert_of_Chirbury "Henry Herbert, 4th Baron Herbert of Chirbury") at Ludlow in March 1689 to oppose [James II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England") and to take part in the imminent war with France.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-nam-41) The regiment continued to have ties with the town of Ludlow, and its successor battalion in The [Royal Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Welsh "Royal Welsh") regiment was granted the freedom of the town in 2014.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-42)

### 18th and 19th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 18th and 19th centuries")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Broad_Gate%2C_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1744340.jpg/250px-Broad_Gate%2C_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1744340.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Broad_Gate,_Ludlow_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1744340.jpg)

Ludlow had seven gates in its town walls; the only one remaining is the Broad Gate (viewed from the south).

The town contained several [coaching inns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coaching_inn "Coaching inn"), [public houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_house "Public house") and [ale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ale "Ale") houses, leading to court records of some alcohol-induced violence and a certain reputation for excess. Several coaching inns were constructed to accommodate travellers by [stagecoach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagecoach "Stagecoach") and [mail coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail_coach "Mail coach"). The Angel on Broad Street was one such notable coaching inn, where several passenger and mail coaches departed and arrived on a regular basis every week, including the _Aurora_ coach which departed for London (taking 27 hours in 1822).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-43) The Angel was the last coaching inn in Ludlow to have such coach traffic, following the arrival of the railways in 1852.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-44) The Angel ceased trading in the early 1990s, though was revived in 2018 as a wine bar occupying a front part of the original establishment. A surviving medieval coaching inn today is the 15th century [Bull Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bull_Hotel,_Ludlow "The Bull Hotel, Ludlow") on the Bull Ring. Several other pubs and hotels in the town have historic pedigree, including the Rose and Crown where allegedly a pub has existed since 1102.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-45)

[Glove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glove "Glove") manufacture was a major industry of the town, peaking in production in 1814.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-46)

In 1802, [Horatio Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Nelson "Horatio Nelson") was awarded the freedom of the borough and stayed at The Angel coaching inn on Broad Street, together with his mistress [Emma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma,_Lady_Hamilton "Emma, Lady Hamilton") and her husband Sir [William Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton_(diplomat) "William Hamilton (diplomat)"). The honour was presented to him in a room at the inn, later to be known as the Nelson Room, and he addressed the crowds from one of the bay windows on the first floor.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-47) During the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars"), [Lucien Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Bonaparte "Lucien Bonaparte"), younger brother of the French Emperor, and his family were imprisoned at Dinham House in 1811.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-48)

In 1832 Thomas Lloyd, the Ludlow doctor and amateur geologist, met [Roderick Murchison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roderick_Murchison "Roderick Murchison") at [Ludford Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford_Corner "Ludford Corner") to study the rocks exposed along the [River Teme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Teme "River Teme") and on Whitcliffe, advancing Murchison's theory for a Silurian System that he was to publish in 1839.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-49) Immediately above the topmost layer of the marine rock sequence forming Murchison's [Silurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silurian "Silurian") System was a thin layer of dark sand containing numerous remains of early fish, especially their scales, along with plant debris, [spores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spores "Spores") and [microscopic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microscopic "Microscopic")[mites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mites "Mites"). In contrast to the underlying sediments of the [Ludlow Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_Series "Ludlow Series") which were deposited in a shallow warm sea some 400 million years ago, the Ludlow [Bone Bed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_Bed "Bone Bed") represents terrestrial (land) conditions and thus a fundamental change in the landscape. At the time, this was believed to be the earliest occurrence of life on land. Murchison thus took the Ludlow Bone Bed as the base of his [Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian "Devonian") System, although over a century later this boundary was to be moved a little higher, the overlying rocks being ascribed to the [Pridoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pridoli_epoch "Pridoli epoch"). The science of [geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology "Geology") has taken a number of local names from these studies and now applies them worldwide, in recognition of the importance of this area to scientific understanding, for example, Ludlow Series. The site is now an [SSSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSSI "SSSI") (Site of Special Scientific Interest) and still attracts international studies.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-50) The [geological interval of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supereon_(geology) "Supereon (geology)"), the [Ludlow Epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_epoch "Ludlow epoch"), is named after the town as part of the [Silurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silurian "Silurian") Period.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-51)

### Recent history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Recent history")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/31/Ludlow_shopper.jpg/250px-Ludlow_shopper.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ludlow_shopper.jpg)

A greengrocers' shop amidst Ludlow's narrow streets.

By the late 20th century, the town had seen a growth in tourism, leading to the appearance of many [antique dealers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antique_dealer "Antique dealer"), as well as [art dealers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_dealer "Art dealer") and independent bookshops (the latter now mostly gone). Bodenhams, a clothing retailer, has been trading from a 600-year-old timbered building since 1860 and is one of the oldest stores in Britain.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-52) Ludlow was described by _[Country Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country\_Life\_(magazine) "Country Life (magazine)")_ as "the most vibrant small town in England."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-53)

A long battle of words between local activists (including many of the town's independent businesses) and [Tesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesco "Tesco") was eventually solved when the mega retailer obtained planning permission to build a supermarket on Corve Street, on the northern edge of the town centre, but only after agreeing to conform to the architectural demands of the local council. The building is designed to follow the outline of the hills in the background, with a curving roof. An [Aldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldi "Aldi") supermarket was subsequently constructed on a site over the road from Tesco.

A development of 91 houses by South Shropshire Housing Association at Rocks Green won a Sustainable Housing award in 2009,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-54) and a [Sainsbury's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainsbury's "Sainsbury's") supermarket at Rocks Green was opened in 2021.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-Sainsburys-55)

In 1983 a small computer magazine started publication in Ludlow by Roger Kean, [Oliver Frey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Frey "Oliver Frey") and Franco Frey by [Newsfield Publications Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsfield_Publications_Ltd "Newsfield Publications Ltd") called [Crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crash_(magazine) "Crash (magazine)"). The magazine catered for the various owners of the [ZX Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX_Spectrum "ZX Spectrum"), and its sister magazine _[Zzap!64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zzap!64 "Zzap!64")_ catered for [Commodore's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_International "Commodore International") rival machine [the C64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_64 "Commodore 64"). The magazine was extremely popular and became Britain's biggest-selling computer magazine in 1986 selling over 100,000 copies monthly. In 1991 Newsfield suffered financial difficulty and the magazines were sold and relaunched by [Europress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europress "Europress").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-56)

In 2004 funding was granted by Advantage West Midlands to build a new 'Eco-Park' on the outskirts of the town on the east side of the [A49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A49_road "A49 road") bypass, at the [Sheet Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet,_Shropshire "Sheet, Shropshire") roundabout, with space for traditional handcraft businesses, new environmentally friendly office buildings and a [park & ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_&_ride "Park & ride") facility. More construction work began in 2006 on the west side of the roundabout on a much-debated pasture land on the town's fringe known as the Foldgate. The land has now been turned over to commercial use with a [filling station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filling_station "Filling station"), [Travelodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travelodge "Travelodge") hotel and [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pub_chain "Pub chain") pub/restaurant, opened in late 2008.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-57)

[Ludlow Distillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_whisky_distilleries_in_England#Ludlow_Distillery "List of whisky distilleries in England") was established in 2009, originally to produce brandy, and now also whisky and gin.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-58)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Ludlow_Castle_from_the_hills.JPG/250px-Ludlow_Castle_from_the_hills.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ludlow_Castle_from_the_hills.JPG)

The town and castle viewed from the Whitcliffe, looking northeast; [Brown Clee Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Clee_Hill "Brown Clee Hill") looms in the distance.

The medieval settlement is largely on the top of a hill, with the castle, market place and parish church (St Laurence's) situated along the flat land on this hilltop, which has a maximum elevation of 111 metres (364 ft) at the castle, falling only gradually towards the east, with an elevation of 107 metres (351 ft) at the Buttercross.

The streets then run down to the Rivers [Teme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Teme "River Teme") and [Corve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Corve "River Corve") (their confluence being to the northwest of the centre of Ludlow) to the north and south. The surface of the Teme has an approximate elevation of 76 metres (249 ft) as it passes Ludford Bridge.

In the western part of the historic core, Dinham retains the character of a village, though dominated by the castle, with a road leading steeply down from Castle Square to the Teme and then over Dinham Bridge (an early 19th century replacement of an older bridge very slightly downstream). The old chapel in Dinham, a Grade II* [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-59) though no longer used for worship, features the oldest built structure in Ludlow outside the castle. To the east a rolling landscape exists, and it is in this direction that the town has steadily grown. [East Hamlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Hamlet "East Hamlet") was the name of the settlement to the east of the town.

The growth of the town in this eastwards (and to the north-east) direction continues to the present day, with little or no development especially to the south or west, to an extent that the traditional town centre (the medieval town) is actually in the southwest corner of the entire settlement. It has also meant that the village of [Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire"), immediately on the other side of the Teme at Ludford Bridge (itself at the foot of Lower Broad Street), remains a distinct community.

Localities in the town's suburbs include Gallows Bank and Sandpits. Immediately beyond the A49 by-pass are Rocks Green and [the Sheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet,_Shropshire "Sheet, Shropshire"), and it is in these two places that much of the present development and growth of the town is taking place, including a Sainsbury's supermarket at Rocks Green.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-Sainsburys-55) They are both approximately 1 mile (1.6 km) from the town centre.

### Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Accolades")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Ludlow_Castle_as_seen_from_the_tower_of_St.Laurence%27s_Church.jpg/250px-Ludlow_Castle_as_seen_from_the_tower_of_St.Laurence%27s_Church.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ludlow_Castle_as_seen_from_the_tower_of_St.Laurence's_Church.jpg)

View from St Laurence's to the castle, looking west across the highest part of the medieval town.

The town has regularly been held in high esteem by academics and commentators in the areas of [urbanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanism "Urbanism") and architecture. Ludlow was winner of _The Great Town Award_ (UK & Ireland) from The Academy of Urbanism in 2007.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-60) The first episode of the BBC television series _[Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TOWN\_with\_Nicholas\_Crane "TOWN with Nicholas Crane")_, in which geographer [Nicholas Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Crane "Nicholas Crane") examines the great towns of the United Kingdom, focused solely on Ludlow for the hour-long documentary.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-61) Ludlow also was one of the _Six English Towns_, a 1977 television programme by architectural historian [Alec Clifton-Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Clifton-Taylor "Alec Clifton-Taylor").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-63)

The historic centre of Ludlow has largely escaped development that would otherwise alter its medieval, Tudor and Georgian character. Furthermore, the lack of development to the south and west allows for the town's historic setting (and particularly that of the castle) by the Teme and the neighbouring countryside to be readily appreciated in the modern day. [M.R.G. Conzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M.R.G._Conzen "M.R.G. Conzen") remarked of Ludlow "Its composite medieval town plan and a history of eight and a half centuries with several periods of considerable importance have endowed its Old Town with an historically well-stratified and richly textured landscape."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-64) Michael Raven, who created a detailed gazetteer of all the settlements of Herefordshire and Shropshire in the late 20th century, stated that "There can be little doubt that Ludlow is the finest town in Shropshire."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-65)

The medieval street plan remains, though the town walls and gates have disappeared in many places. Mill Street and Broad Street, leading down from the very centre to the Teme in the south, are particularly famous for their rich architectural heritage and vistas, with many fine Georgian buildings. Sir [Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner") described Broad Street as "one of the most memorable streets in England".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-66)

## Population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Population")]

The [2011 UK census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census_in_the_United_Kingdom "Census in the United Kingdom") recorded 10,266 people living in Ludlow's [civil parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_parishes_in_England "Civil parishes in England").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-67) A further 673 live in the neighbouring [Ludford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford,_Shropshire "Ludford, Shropshire") parish to the south,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-68) meaning the population for the town and adjoining settlements is approximately 11,000. The 2021 Census showed a population of 10,039 in Ludlow parish and still 673 in Ludford parish, giving a total of 10,712, plus about a further 1,000 in neighbouring parishes within the three county wards of Ludlow East, North and South.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Transport")]

### Railways

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Railways")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Ludlow_railway_station_-_DSCF2178.JPG/250px-Ludlow_railway_station_-_DSCF2178.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ludlow_railway_station_-_DSCF2178.JPG)

The southbound platform at Ludlow station

[Ludlow railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow_railway_station "Ludlow railway station") began serving the town in 1852 and is about five minutes' walk from the town centre. It is on the [Welsh Marches Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Marches_Line "Welsh Marches Line") and is served by trains between [Manchester Piccadilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Piccadilly_railway_station "Manchester Piccadilly railway station"), [Crewe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crewe_railway_station "Crewe railway station"), [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury_railway_station "Shrewsbury railway station"), [Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereford_railway_station "Hereford railway station"), [Abergavenny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abergavenny_railway_station "Abergavenny railway station"), [Cardiff Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_Central_railway_station "Cardiff Central railway station") and [Swansea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swansea_railway_station "Swansea railway station"); these are operated by [Transport for Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_Wales_Rail "Transport for Wales Rail").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-73)

There is a short tunnel to the south of the station, which runs under Gravel Hill. [Clee Hill Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clee_Hill_Junction "Clee Hill Junction") existed just to the north of the station, with a goods line leading off the main line up to the quarries on [Titterstone Clee Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titterstone_Clee_Hill "Titterstone Clee Hill").

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Coach%2C_Mill_Street%2C_Ludlow_-_IMG_0226.JPG/250px-Coach%2C_Mill_Street%2C_Ludlow_-_IMG_0226.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coach,_Mill_Street,_Ludlow_-_IMG_0226.JPG)

Bus services in the area are operated by [Diamond Bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_West_Midlands "Diamond West Midlands"), Lugg Valley Travel and [Minsterley Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minsterley_Motors "Minsterley Motors"). Routes link the town with Church Stretton, [Kidderminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidderminster "Kidderminster") and Shrewsbury; there is also a [park and ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_and_ride_bus_services_in_the_United_Kingdom "Park and ride bus services in the United Kingdom") service, on a circular route.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-74)

### Roads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Roads")]

On 4 February 1980, the £4.7 million single-carriageway [by-pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bypass_(road) "Bypass (road)") road was officially opened by [Kenneth Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Clarke "Kenneth Clarke"). The by-pass had been built to the east of Ludlow in the late 1970s, opening to traffic in the summer of 1979, and diverts the [A49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A49_road "A49 road")[trunk road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trunk_road "Trunk road") around the town. The former route of the A49 through the town was reclassified as the B4361.

The town centre retains its medieval streets and has had long-running problems with motor traffic and car parking, which is now restricted seven days a week. There is a town centre residents' parking permit scheme in operation. Council-owned car parks exist in a number of locations in Ludlow to cater for much of the long-stay car parking. The Eco-Park is situated on the eastern outskirts of the town, at [the Sheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet,_Shropshire "Sheet, Shropshire") and adjacent to the A49.

The [A4117](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A4117_road "A4117 road") begins at the Rocks Green roundabout on the Ludlow by-pass and runs across the [Clee Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clee_Hills "Clee Hills") to [Cleobury Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleobury_Mortimer "Cleobury Mortimer"); it then continues via the [A456](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A456_road "A456 road") onwards to [Bewdley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bewdley "Bewdley") and Kidderminster.

Two historic bridges cross the [River Teme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Teme "River Teme") at Ludlow: [Ludford Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludford_Bridge "Ludford Bridge") (a Scheduled Ancient Monument) and Dinham Bridge (early 19th century, Grade II listed);[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-75) both of which still take vehicular traffic as no modern bridges have been built over the Teme in the area. To the north of the town centre, the historic Corve Bridge crosses the River Corve and this bridge was relieved by [Burway Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burway_Bridge "Burway Bridge") in the mid-20th century. However, on 26 June 2007, [dramatic flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_United_Kingdom_floods "2007 United Kingdom floods") on the Corve caused the Burway Bridge to collapse, severing a gas main and causing 20 homes in nearby Corve Street to be evacuated.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludlow#cite_note-76) The old stone bridge has now been replaced with a modern steel and pre-fabricated concrete construction.

### Cycling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ludlow&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Cycling")]

[National Cycle Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cycle_Network "National Cycle Network")[route 44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cycle_Route_44 "National Cycle Route 44") runs over Dinham and Ludford Bridges (via Camp and Silkmill Lanes in-between) en route from Bromfield to [Pipe Aston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipe_Aston "Pipe Aston"). It is known as the _Six Castles Cycleway_, with Ludlow Castle as one of the six.
